title: Supply Chain Attack
summary: A supply chain attack is an intrusion that reaches a target indirectly by compromising something the target trusts: a software dependency, a build system, a package registry, an update mechanism, a managed service provider, or a hardware or firmware supplier. The attraction for an adversary is leverage. One compromised package or build job can yield access to thousands of downstream organisations, and the resulting code or update often arrives already signed, already approved and already allow-listed. Documented patterns include malicious package versions published to public registries, typosquatted and dependency-confusion package names that resolve to attacker-controlled artifacts, compromised maintainer accounts, injected code in build pipelines that never touches the repository, and tampered vendor updates delivered through legitimate channels. For a practising engineer the defences are layered and mostly about provenance rather than detection: pin and verify dependencies with lock files and integrity hashes, generate and review build provenance, require signed artifacts with verification at install and deploy time, restrict who can publish and with what credentials, and monitor registries and build systems as production infrastructure. Attribution is genuinely hard because the activity happens inside trusted workflows; logs from build systems, registry publish events and artifact signing services often provide the only visibility. The most common organisational failure is assuming that internal dependence on well-known vendors removes the risk, when in practice the exposure is determined by how much unverified code and configuration is consumed, and how quickly a compromised component could be identified and removed from production.
objectives: You will be able to describe the main supply chain attack patterns, including malicious packages, dependency confusion, compromised maintainers and build pipeline injection.
You will be able to explain why signed and approved artifacts still require verification and provenance checks rather than blind trust.
You will be able to design controls for dependency pinning, integrity verification and registry allow-listing.
You will be able to specify telemetry from build systems, package registries and signing services that would reveal a compromised build.
You will be able to assess an organisation's time to identify and remove a compromised dependency from production.
You will be able to distinguish third-party and vendor risk that is genuinely mitigated from assurance that rests on reputation alone.
